pages.title: What you will learn
pages.body:
🎯 **By the end of this lesson you will be able to:**
- Identify and name chemical compounds from a collection of materials commonly found at home, school and the community, such as table salt, water, vinegar, fuel, soap, detergents, marble and fertilisers.
- Write the chemical symbols of the elements identified in the chemical compounds.

pages.title: What is a Binary Chemical Compound?
pages.body: A binary chemical compound is a compound formed from exactly two different elements chemically combined together. Many everyday materials found at home, school and in the community are actually binary compounds, even though we usually refer to them by their common names rather than their chemical names. Recognising these materials as chemical compounds is an important first step in understanding the chemistry of the world around us.

lessons.subject: sci
lessons.title: Common Materials and the Compounds They Contain

pages.title: Common Materials and the Compounds They Contain
pages.body:
Table salt, water, vinegar, marble and fertiliser are examples of everyday materials that are, or contain, binary or related chemical compounds, along with their common uses, as summarised in the table below.

| **MATERIAL** | **CHEMICAL NAME OR CONTENT** | **COMMON USE** |
|---|---|---|
| **Table salt** | Sodium chloride | Seasoning food and preserving food |
| **Water** | Hydrogen oxide | Drinking, cooking, cleaning, and supporting all life processes |
| **Vinegar** | Contains acetic acid | Flavouring and preserving food |
| **Fuel (petrol, kerosene)** | Mainly hydrocarbon compounds, formed from carbon and hydrogen | Powering vehicles, generators and lamps. Handle with care and keep away from flames |
| **Soap** | Sodium or potassium salts of fatty acids | Washing and personal hygiene |
| **Detergents** | Contain sulphonate or similar cleaning compounds | Washing clothes and cleaning surfaces |
| **Marble** | Calcium carbonate | Building construction and making cement |
| **Fertiliser** | Often contains ammonium compounds | Supplying nutrients to crops to improve growth |

pages.title: Chemical Symbols of the First Twenty Elements
pages.body:
A chemical symbol is a short form, usually one or two letters, used to represent an element in chemical formulas and equations. Most symbols are simply drawn from the first one or two letters of the element's name, and learning the symbols of the first twenty elements of the periodic table, listed in the table below, gives a strong foundation for reading and writing chemical formulas confidently.

pages.title: Elements Whose Symbols Come from Latin Names
pages.body:
Not every chemical symbol matches the first letters of the element's modern English name. A small group of elements, most of them metals known and used since ancient times, keep symbols based on their old Latin names instead. Sodium and potassium, both within the first twenty elements, belong to this group, and so do several familiar metals found beyond the first twenty, including iron, copper, silver, gold, tin, lead, mercury, antimony and tungsten. The table below lists each of these elements alongside the Latin name its symbol is drawn from, together with a common everyday use.

| **ELEMENT** | **SYMBOL** | **LATIN NAME** | **COMMON USE** |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Sodium** | Na | Natrium | Found in table salt and in body fluids |
| **Potassium** | K | Kalium | Found in bananas, important for nerves and muscles |
| **Iron** | Fe | Ferrum | Used to make tools, nails and building frames |
| **Copper** | Cu | Cuprum | Used in electrical wiring and water pipes |
| **Silver** | Ag | Argentum | Used in jewellery and electrical contacts |
| **Gold** | Au | Aurum | Used in jewellery because it resists corrosion |
| **Tin** | Sn | Stannum | Used to coat steel cans to prevent rusting |
| **Lead** | Pb | Plumbum | Used in car batteries and radiation shielding |
| **Mercury** | Hg | Hydrargyrum | Used in some thermometers and switches |
| **Antimony** | Sb | Stibium | Used to harden lead in batteries and alloys |
| **Tungsten** | W | Wolfram | Used in light bulb filaments and cutting tools |

Notice that these Latin derived symbols are not random. Sodium's symbol, Na, comes directly from natrium, iron's symbol, Fe, comes from ferrum, and gold's symbol, Au, comes from aurum. Knowing this small group of exceptions well is useful, since these elements appear repeatedly throughout chemistry, from simple compounds studied at this level to more advanced work in later grades.

[[pic:A labelled poster style image showing the periodic table symbols of the first twenty elements grouped clearly by period and group, with a separate highlighted panel showing the eleven elements whose symbols come from Latin names, each paired with its everyday metal object (for example a copper wire, an iron nail, and a gold ring).]]

Notice that each compound studied so far in this lesson is made of exactly two different elements. Water is made of hydrogen and oxygen, carbon (IV) oxide is made of carbon and oxygen, iron (II) sulphide is made of iron and sulphur, and magnesium oxide is made of magnesium and oxygen. This is what makes each of them a binary compound.

pages.title: Formulae of Common Compounds at Home, School and in the Community
pages.body:
| **MATERIAL** | **CHEMICAL NAME AND FORMULA** | **ELEMENTS PRESENT** | **BINARY COMPOUND?** |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Table salt** | Sodium chloride, NaCl | Sodium (Na) and chlorine (Cl) | Yes |
| **Water** | Water, H₂O | Hydrogen (H) and oxygen (O) | Yes |
| **Gas breathed out** | Carbon (IV) oxide, CO₂ | Carbon (C) and oxygen (O) | Yes |
| **Quicklime** | Calcium oxide, CaO | Calcium (Ca) and oxygen (O) | Yes |
| **Ammonia in some fertilisers and cleaners** | Ammonia, NH₃ | Nitrogen (N) and hydrogen (H) | Yes |
| **Marble and limestone** | Calcium carbonate, CaCO₃ | Calcium (Ca), carbon (C) and oxygen (O) | No, it has three elements |
| **Vinegar** | Ethanoic acid in water, CH₃COOH | Carbon (C), hydrogen (H) and oxygen (O) | No, it has three elements |
| **Fertiliser** | Ammonium sulphate, (NH₄)₂SO₄, and urea, CO(NH₂)₂ | Nitrogen (N), hydrogen (H), oxygen (O) with sulphur (S) or carbon (C) | No |
| **Soap and detergents** | Large compounds of carbon, hydrogen and oxygen with sodium or potassium | Several elements | No |

A binary compound is named by writing the name of the first element followed by the second element with its ending changed to ide. Sodium and chlorine form sodium chloride, magnesium and oxygen form magnesium oxide, and iron and sulphur form iron (II) sulphide. Fuels such as petrol and kerosene are mixtures of compounds of carbon and hydrogen. They catch fire easily and must be kept away from flames.

pages.title: Going further
pages.body:
> 💡 **Going further**

Not every common household material is a binary compound. Some, like table salt (sodium chloride), are indeed binary, made of just two elements, sodium and chlorine. Others, like vinegar, contain more complex compounds made of three or more elements. Recognising which materials are truly binary compounds, and which are mixtures or more complex compounds, is a useful skill that builds directly on the earlier study of mixtures and compounds from previous grades.

pages.title: What you will learn
pages.body:
🎯 **By the end of this lesson you will be able to:**
- Distinguish among elements, molecules, ions and compounds.
- Write molecular formula of binary compounds and describe their formation.
- Compare and contrast different binary chemical compounds based on their composition and properties.
- Form models to represent chemical compounds such as water, carbon (IV) oxide, iron (II) sulphide and magnesium oxide.

pages.title: Elements
pages.body: An element is a pure substance made up of only one type of atom, which cannot be broken down into anything simpler by ordinary chemical means. Elements are the basic building blocks from which every other substance, including every compound studied in this lesson, is ultimately made. Elements that learners encounter often in everyday life include oxygen, which we breathe in the air and which supports burning, nitrogen, which makes up most of the air around us, hydrogen, which is used as a clean burning fuel and is found in water, carbon, which forms the basis of charcoal, diamond and the graphite in pencils, iron, which is used to make tools, nails and the frames of buildings, aluminium, which is used to make cooking pots, drink cans and roofing sheets, copper, which is used in electrical wires because it conducts electricity well, gold, which is used in jewellery because it does not corrode, sulphur, which is found in matches and is responsible for the smell of rotten eggs, and calcium, which is found in bones, teeth and limestone rock.

questions.q: An element is best described as
o: A pure substance made of only one type of atom
A substance made of two different elements only
Two or more atoms of different elements joined together
questions.e: Elements An element is a pure substance made up of only one type of atom, which cannot be broken down into anything simpler by ordinary chemical means.

pages.title: Molecules
pages.body: A molecule is formed when two or more atoms join together by chemical bonds, and these atoms may belong to the same element or to different elements. Molecules that are part of everyday life include water (H2O), which we drink and cook with, oxygen gas (O2), which we breathe in to release energy from food, carbon (IV) oxide (CO2), which we breathe out and which plants use in photosynthesis, nitrogen gas (N2), which makes up about four fifths of the air, methane (CH4), the main gas found in natural gas and biogas, ammonia (NH3), used in cleaning products and to manufacture fertiliser, glucose (C6H12O6), the sugar our bodies use for energy, ozone (O3), a gas high in the atmosphere that protects us from harmful rays from the sun, hydrogen gas (H2), used as a clean fuel, and ethanol (C2H5OH), the alcohol found in some drinks and hand sanitisers. Notice that oxygen gas and ozone are both molecules of the same single element, while water, carbon (IV) oxide and the others listed contain more than one type of element and are therefore also compounds.

pages.title: Ions
pages.body: An ion is an atom or a group of atoms that has gained or lost one or more electrons, giving it an overall electrical charge. Ions commonly referred to in chemistry and in daily life include the sodium ion, found in table salt and in the fluids of the human body, the chloride ion, also found in table salt and in stomach acid, the calcium ion, important for strong bones and teeth, the potassium ion, important for nerve and muscle function and found in bananas, the magnesium ion, found in chlorophyll in green plants, the hydrogen ion, responsible for the acidity of a solution, the hydroxide ion, responsible for the alkalinity of a solution, the iron ion, found in haemoglobin in our blood, the carbonate ion, found in limestone and chalk, and the nitrate ion, found in fertilisers used by farmers. Positively charged ions, such as the sodium and calcium ions, are called cations, while negatively charged ions, such as the chloride and hydroxide ions, are called anions.

pages.title: Compounds
pages.body: A compound is a substance formed when two or more different elements combine chemically in a fixed, definite ratio, producing a new substance with properties different from the elements that formed it. Compounds that learners meet regularly include water (H2O), table salt or sodium chloride (NaCl), carbon (IV) oxide (CO2), used in fizzy drinks and produced by burning, calcium carbonate (CaCO3), the main compound in limestone, marble and chalk, sodium hydroxide (NaOH), used in making soap, sulfuric acid (H2SO4), used in car batteries, ammonia (NH3), used in fertiliser production, glucose (C6H12O6), our main source of energy, iron (II) sulphide (FeS), formed when iron and sulphur react, and magnesium oxide (MgO), used in some antacid medicines. Every one of these compounds is made of at least two different elements chemically joined together, which is what distinguishes a compound from a molecule of a single element such as oxygen gas.

pages.title: Distinguishing the Four Terms
pages.body:
Oxygen gas (O2) is a molecule because it is made of two atoms joined together, but it is not a compound, since both atoms belong to the same element. Water (H2O) is both a molecule and a compound, since it is made of atoms joined together, and those atoms belong to two different elements. The sodium ion (Na+) is neither a molecule nor a compound, since it is a single charged atom rather than atoms joined together. Table salt (NaCl) is a compound made of sodium ions and chloride ions held together by attraction between their opposite charges. Keeping these distinctions clear from the start will help you understand chemical formulas and reactions throughout this lesson and in future studies.

2.3  Writing Molecular Formulas, the Criss Cross Method

Valency, sometimes called combining power, is the number of bonds an atom of a particular element can form with other atoms, and it is the key piece of information needed to work out the correct chemical formula of a binary compound. The criss cross method is a simple, step by step technique that uses valency to write the correct formula of a compound made from two elements.

- Step 1. Write the symbol of each element side by side, with the element that is more like a metal written first.

- Step 2. Write the valency of each element as a small number directly below its symbol.

- Step 3. Cross over the valency numbers, so that the valency of the first element becomes the subscript of the second element, and the valency of the second element becomes the subscript of the first element.

- Step 4. If both subscripts turn out to be the same number, they cancel out and are simply left out of the formula, since a subscript of one is not written.

- Step 5. If both subscripts share a common factor, divide both by that common factor to reduce the formula to its simplest whole number ratio.

- Step 6. Write the final formula using the element symbols together with their reduced subscripts.

Common valencies for frequently used elements are shown in the table below, since knowing these values by heart makes the criss cross method quick and reliable to apply.

| **ELEMENT** | **VALENCY** | **ELEMENT** | **VALENCY** | **ELEMENT** | **VALENCY** |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Hydrogen (H)** | 1 | Sodium (Na) | 1 | Aluminium (Al) | 3 |
| **Oxygen (O)** | 2 | Potassium (K) | 1 | Carbon (C) | 4 |
| **Chlorine (Cl)** | 1 | Calcium (Ca) | 2 | Iron (Fe) | 2 or 3 |
| **Sulphur (S)** | 2 | Magnesium (Mg) | 2 | Zinc (Zn) | 2 |

lessons.subject: sci
lessons.title: Worked Examples of the Criss Cross Method

pages.title: Worked Examples of the Criss Cross Method
pages.body:
Example 1, sodium and chlorine. Sodium has a valency of 1 and chlorine has a valency of 1. Crossing over the valencies gives a subscript of 1 for each element, and since a subscript of 1 is not written, the formula simplifies directly to NaCl.

Example 2, magnesium and chlorine. Magnesium has a valency of 2 and chlorine has a valency of 1. Crossing over the valencies gives chlorine a subscript of 2, while magnesium keeps a subscript of 1, which is not written, giving the formula MgCl2.

Example 3, aluminium and oxygen. Aluminium has a valency of 3 and oxygen has a valency of 2. Crossing over the valencies gives aluminium a subscript of 2 and oxygen a subscript of 3, giving the formula Al2O3, which cannot be simplified further since 2 and 3 share no common factor.

Example 4, calcium and oxygen. Calcium has a valency of 2 and oxygen has a valency of 2. Crossing over the valencies gives both elements a subscript of 2, written as Ca2O2, but since 2 and 2 share a common factor of 2, this is reduced to the simplest ratio, giving the final formula CaO.

pages.title: Practising with More Binary Compounds
pages.body:
Applying the criss cross method to a wider range of common binary compounds gives the formulas and reasoning shown in the table below, expanding on the four compounds highlighted earlier in this lesson.

| **COMPOUND** | **FORMULA** | **HOW IT FORMS (USING VALENCY)** |
|---|---|---|
| **Water** | H2O | Hydrogen (valency 1) and oxygen (valency 2) criss cross to give two hydrogen atoms for every one oxygen atom |
| **Carbon (IV) oxide** | CO2 | Carbon (valency 4) and oxygen (valency 2) criss cross and simplify to give one carbon atom for every two oxygen atoms |
| **Iron (II) sulphide** | FeS | Iron (valency 2) and sulphur (valency 2) criss cross and simplify to a one to one ratio |
| **Magnesium oxide** | MgO | Magnesium (valency 2) and oxygen (valency 2) criss cross and simplify to a one to one ratio |
| **Sodium oxide** | Na2O | Sodium (valency 1) and oxygen (valency 2) criss cross to give two sodium atoms for every one oxygen atom |
| **Calcium chloride** | CaCl2 | Calcium (valency 2) and chlorine (valency 1) criss cross to give one calcium atom for every two chlorine atoms |
| **Aluminium oxide** | Al2O3 | Aluminium (valency 3) and oxygen (valency 2) criss cross to give two aluminium atoms for every three oxygen atoms |
| **Zinc sulphide** | ZnS | Zinc (valency 2) and sulphur (valency 2) criss cross and simplify to a one to one ratio |
| **Potassium iodide** | KI | Potassium (valency 1) and iodine (valency 1) criss cross to a one to one ratio |
| **Hydrogen chloride** | HCl | Hydrogen (valency 1) and chlorine (valency 1) criss cross to a one to one ratio |

2.4  Practical Illustration

[[pic:A set of four labelled ball and stick models, side by side, showing the atoms and bonds in water, carbon (IV) oxide, iron (II) sulphide and magnesium oxide, with each atom colour coded and named.]]

Notice how each model shows the exact atoms that combine to form the compound, matching the molecular formula obtained using the criss cross method. Building simple models like these, using labelled balls, beads or drawings, helps make the invisible process of compound formation easier to visualise and understand.

2.5  Comparing Binary Compounds

Composition, physical state, and relevance to everyday life are useful bases for comparing different binary compounds, as shown in the table below. A table is especially helpful here, since it allows several compounds to be compared side by side across the same set of features at a glance.

| **COMPOUND** | **STATE AT ROOM TEMPERATURE** | **TYPE OF ELEMENTS COMBINED** | **EVERYDAY RELEVANCE** |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Water (H2O)** | Liquid | Two nonmetals (hydrogen and oxygen) | Essential for drinking, cooking and all life processes |
| **Carbon (IV) oxide (CO2)** | Gas | Two nonmetals (carbon and oxygen) | Produced by respiration and burning, used by plants in photosynthesis |
| **Iron (II) sulphide (FeS)** | Solid | A metal and a nonmetal (iron and sulphur) | Formed when iron reacts with sulphur, used in laboratory demonstrations |
| **Magnesium oxide (MgO)** | Solid | A metal and a nonmetal (magnesium and oxygen) | Used in antacid medicines and as a heat resistant lining material |

Notice that water and carbon (IV) oxide are both formed from two nonmetals, yet one is a liquid and the other is a gas at room temperature, showing that composition alone does not determine every property of a compound. Similarly, iron (II) sulphide and magnesium oxide are both formed from a metal and a nonmetal, but they have very different appearances, uses and chemical behaviours, showing that even compounds with a similar general pattern of composition can differ significantly in their specific properties.

pages.title: Elements, Molecules, Ions and Compounds Compared
pages.body:
| **TERM** | **MEANING** | **EXAMPLES** |
|---|---|---|
| **Element** | A substance made of only one kind of atom, which cannot be split into simpler substances by chemical means | Iron (Fe), sulphur (S), oxygen (O) |
| **Molecule** | Two or more atoms joined together by sharing electrons. The atoms may be the same or different | O₂, H₂, H₂O, CO₂ |
| **Ion** | An atom or group of atoms that carries a charge because it has lost or gained electrons | Na⁺, Mg²⁺, Cl⁻, O²⁻ |
| **Compound** | A substance in which two or more different elements are chemically combined in a fixed proportion | NaCl, H₂O, MgO, FeS |

pages.title: How Four Binary Compounds are Formed
pages.body:
| **COMPOUND** | **HOW IT IS FORMED** | **WHAT IS OBSERVED** | **WORD EQUATION** |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Water, H₂O** | Hydrogen burns in oxygen. Two hydrogen atoms share electrons with one oxygen atom | A colourless liquid forms | Hydrogen + oxygen gives water |
| **Carbon (IV) oxide, CO₂** | Carbon, as charcoal, burns in plenty of air. One carbon atom shares electrons with two oxygen atoms | A colourless gas forms that turns limewater milky | Carbon + oxygen gives carbon (IV) oxide |
| **Magnesium oxide, MgO** | Magnesium ribbon burns in air. Each magnesium atom gives two electrons to an oxygen atom | A bright white flame, then a white powder | Magnesium + oxygen gives magnesium oxide |
| **Iron (II) sulphide, FeS** | A mixture of iron filings and sulphur powder is heated strongly. Each iron atom gives two electrons to a sulphur atom | The mixture glows red and a black solid forms that a magnet does not attract | Iron + sulphur gives iron (II) sulphide |

A compound has properties that are different from those of its elements. Iron is attracted by a magnet and sulphur is a yellow powder, but iron (II) sulphide is a black solid that is not magnetic. Water is a liquid that puts out fire, although hydrogen burns and oxygen supports burning. To model these compounds, use balls of clay of different colours for the atoms and short sticks for the bonds.

pages.title: Going further
pages.body:
> 💡 **Going further**

Understanding the difference between elements, molecules, ions and compounds, together with confidence in the criss cross method, forms the foundation for balancing chemical equations and predicting the products of chemical reactions in more advanced chemistry studies. A common error among learners is confusing a molecule of an element, such as oxygen gas, with a compound, simply because it contains more than one atom. Remembering that a true compound must always contain at least two different elements helps avoid this confusion.

lessons.subject: sci
lessons.title: Characteristics of Acids, Bases and Salts

pages.title: What you will learn
pages.body:
🎯 **By the end of this lesson you will be able to:**
- Identify acids, bases and salts by their characteristics.
- Create a model of a pH scale and use it to determine the strength of common acids and alkali solutions using indicators.

pages.title: Strong and Weak Acids and Bases
pages.body:
Every acid and every base can be described not only by what it is, but also by how strong it is, and this idea of strength is central to understanding the pH scale used throughout this lesson. A strong acid is one that breaks apart almost completely when dissolved in water, releasing a large number of hydrogen ions and producing a very low pH, usually between 0 and 3. Hydrochloric acid, sulfuric acid and nitric acid are common examples of strong acids. A weak acid, by contrast, only partly breaks apart in water, releasing far fewer hydrogen ions and producing a pH closer to the middle of the scale, usually between 4 and 6. Ethanoic acid (found in vinegar) and carbonic acid (found in fizzy drinks) are common examples of weak acids.

In the same way, a strong base is one that breaks apart almost completely in water, releasing a large number of hydroxide ions and producing a very high pH, usually between 11 and 14. Sodium hydroxide and potassium hydroxide are common examples of strong bases. A weak base only partly breaks apart in water, releasing fewer hydroxide ions and producing a pH closer to the middle of the scale, usually between 8 and 10. Ammonia solution is the most common example of a weak base met at this level. Strength should never be confused with concentration, since even a small, dilute amount of a strong acid can still be far more reactive than a large, concentrated amount of a weak acid, because strength describes how completely the acid breaks apart, not how much of it is present.

[[pic:A horizontal pH scale bar numbered 0 to 14, colour graded from red at the acidic end through green at neutral (pH 7) to purple at the alkaline end, with labelled examples placed at their approximate position, for example lemon juice near pH 2, vinegar near pH 3, pure water at pH 7, and soap solution near pH 10.]]

Notice how the scale runs from the strongest acids at the lowest numbers, through neutral at pH 7, to the strongest bases at the highest numbers. Strong acids and strong bases sit at the extreme ends of the scale, while weak acids and weak bases sit closer to the middle, on either side of neutral.

3.4  Acids

questions.q: A weak base is one that
o: Only partly breaks apart in water, releasing fewer hydroxide ions
questions.e: A weak base only partly breaks apart in water, releasing fewer hydroxide ions and producing a pH closer to the middle of the scale, usually between 8 and 10.

questions.q: Ammonia solution is an example of an
questions.e: Ammonia solution is the most common example of a weak base met at this level.

pages.title: What is an Acid?
pages.body: An acid is a substance that releases hydrogen ions when dissolved in water, giving it a pH below 7 and a range of recognisable properties. Acids are found throughout nature, in our food, and in industry, and can be classified by where they come from into organic acids and inorganic acids.

pages.title: Classifying Acids by Source
pages.body:
Organic acids are acids that contain carbon and are generally produced by living organisms or found naturally in plant and animal materials, and they are usually weak acids. Examples of organic acids include ethanoic acid, found in vinegar, citric acid, found in oranges, lemons and other citrus fruits, lactic acid, found in sour milk and produced in muscles during hard exercise, tartaric acid, found in grapes and used in baking powder, malic acid, found in apples, formic acid, found in the bites and stings of ants and nettles, ascorbic acid, also known as vitamin C and found in citrus fruits and vegetables, oxalic acid, found in spinach and rhubarb, butyric acid, responsible for the smell of rancid butter, and benzoic acid, used as a food preservative.

Inorganic acids, sometimes called mineral acids, do not contain carbon in their basic structure and are generally manufactured industrially, though a few occur naturally. They are often, though not always, strong acids. Examples of inorganic acids include hydrochloric acid, found naturally in the stomach and used industrially to clean metal surfaces, sulfuric acid, used in car batteries and in manufacturing fertiliser, nitric acid, used in manufacturing fertiliser and explosives, phosphoric acid, used in soft drinks and rust removers, carbonic acid, formed when carbon (IV) oxide dissolves in water and found in fizzy drinks, boric acid, used as a mild antiseptic, hydrofluoric acid, used to etch glass, hydrobromic acid, used in industry to manufacture other chemicals, sulfurous acid, used as a preservative and bleaching agent, and nitrous acid, used in the manufacture of dyes.

questions.q: Ethanoic acid, found in vinegar, is classified as an
questions.e: Examples of organic acids include ethanoic acid, found in vinegar, citric acid, found in oranges, lemons and other citrus fruits, lactic acid, found in sour milk and produced in muscles during hard exercise, tartaric acid, found…

questions.q: Hydrochloric acid is classified as an
questions.e: Examples of inorganic acids include hydrochloric acid, found naturally in the stomach and used industrially to clean metal surfaces, sulfuric acid, used in car batteries and in manufacturing fertiliser, nitric acid, used in…

pages.title: Physical Properties of Acids
pages.body: Acids generally taste sour, which is why lemons and vinegar taste sharp on the tongue, though tasting unknown laboratory chemicals is never a safe way to test this. Acids are usually soluble in water, forming solutions that conduct electricity due to the free ions present. Most acids are colourless liquids or solids that dissolve to form colourless or lightly coloured solutions, and many acids give off a sharp, pungent smell, particularly concentrated inorganic acids.

pages.title: Chemical Properties of Acids
pages.body: Acids turn blue litmus paper red, which is one of the simplest laboratory tests used to identify them. Acids react with reactive metals, such as zinc, magnesium and iron, to produce a salt and hydrogen gas, which can be tested for using a lit splint that produces a characteristic pop sound. Acids react with metal carbonates, such as calcium carbonate, to produce a salt, water and carbon (IV) oxide gas, which turns limewater milky. Acids react with bases in a neutralisation reaction to produce a salt and water. Acids also react with metal oxides in a similar neutralisation reaction, again producing a salt and water.

questions.q: Which of the following is a chemical property of acids?
o: Have no reaction with metal carbonates
React with metals to produce a salt and hydrogen gas
questions.e: Acids react with reactive metals, such as zinc, magnesium and iron, to produce a salt and hydrogen gas, which can be tested for using a lit splint that produces a characteristic pop sound.

pages.title: Uses of Acids
pages.body:
Acids have several common, specific uses that make them essential in daily life and industry. Hydrochloric acid is used to clean metal surfaces before galvanising or soldering. Sulfuric acid is used in car batteries to allow the battery to store and release electrical energy. Nitric acid is used in the manufacture of fertilisers that help crops grow. Ethanoic acid, as vinegar, is used to flavour and preserve food such as pickles. Citric acid is used as a natural preservative and flavouring in soft drinks and sweets. Carbonic acid gives fizzy drinks their bubbles. Ascorbic acid, as vitamin C, is added to foods and taken as a supplement to support the immune system. Phosphoric acid is used in some soft drinks and in rust removing products. Boric acid is used as a mild antiseptic for minor cuts. Lactic acid is used in the food industry to preserve and flavour products such as yoghurt.

3.5  Bases

pages.title: What is a Base?
pages.body: A base is a substance that can neutralise an acid, often by releasing hydroxide ions when dissolved in water, giving it a pH above 7. A base that dissolves in water to form a solution is more specifically called an alkali, and every alkali is a base, though not every base is soluble enough in water to be described this way.

pages.title: Classifying Bases by Source
pages.body:
Inorganic bases are generally metal hydroxides or metal oxides, manufactured or mined, and are often strong bases. Examples of inorganic bases include sodium hydroxide, used in soap making, potassium hydroxide, used in liquid soaps and some batteries, calcium hydroxide, also called slaked lime and used to reduce soil acidity, magnesium hydroxide, used in antacid medicines as milk of magnesia, calcium oxide, also called quicklime and used in cement production, sodium carbonate, also called washing soda and used in cleaning products, potassium carbonate, used in glass and soap manufacture, zinc oxide, used in skin ointments, iron (III) hydroxide, formed as rust in the presence of moisture, and copper (II) hydroxide, used in some fungicides for crops.

Organic bases are generally derived from living organisms, contain nitrogen, and are usually weaker bases. Examples of organic bases include ammonia, produced naturally from decaying plant and animal matter and used in cleaning products, methylamine, found in decaying fish, quinine, a bitter compound from cinchona bark once used to treat malaria, caffeine, found in coffee, tea and cocoa, nicotine, found in tobacco plants, morphine, a pain relieving compound from the opium poppy, codeine, a related pain relieving compound found in the same plant, histamine, produced by the body during allergic reactions, urea, found in urine and used as a fertiliser, and adrenaline, a hormone produced naturally by the body.

pages.title: Physical Properties of Bases
pages.body: Bases generally taste bitter, feel slippery or soapy to the touch, and many are white, crystalline solids at room temperature, though a few, such as ammonia solution, are colourless liquids. Bases that dissolve in water form alkaline solutions that conduct electricity, similar to acids, due to the free ions present.

pages.title: Chemical Properties of Bases
pages.body: Bases turn red litmus paper blue, providing a simple laboratory test for identifying them. Bases react with acids in a neutralisation reaction to produce a salt and water. Bases react with certain metal salt solutions to produce an insoluble metal hydroxide, seen as a precipitate, which is a common test used to identify particular metal ions in solution. Some bases, especially ammonia solution, react with concentrated acids to produce dense white fumes of ammonium salts, another useful identification test.

pages.title: Uses of Bases
pages.body:
Bases have several common, specific uses in daily life and industry. Sodium hydroxide is used in the manufacture of soap and paper. Calcium hydroxide, as slaked lime, is spread on farmland to reduce soil acidity before planting. Magnesium hydroxide, as milk of magnesia, is used to relieve indigestion and excess stomach acid. Ammonia solution is used as a household cleaning agent for glass and surfaces. Potassium hydroxide is used to make liquid soaps and some types of batteries. Sodium carbonate, as washing soda, is used to soften water and remove grease. Calcium oxide is used in the production of cement and mortar for building. Zinc oxide is used in ointments to protect and heal skin. Urea, a mild organic base, is used as a fertiliser to supply nitrogen to crops. Ammonium hydroxide, formed when ammonia dissolves in water, is used in some hair treatment products.

3.6  Salts

pages.title: What is a Salt?
pages.body: A salt is a compound formed when the hydrogen ion of an acid is wholly or partly replaced by a metal ion or an ammonium ion, most commonly through a neutralisation reaction between an acid and a base. Salts are classified into four main types based on how completely the acid and base have reacted together.

pages.title: Normal Salts
pages.body: A normal salt is formed when all of the replaceable hydrogen ions of an acid are completely replaced by metal or ammonium ions, leaving no acidic hydrogen behind. Examples of normal salts include sodium chloride (table salt), potassium nitrate (used in fertiliser and gunpowder), calcium sulphate (found in gypsum and plaster of Paris), sodium carbonate (washing soda), potassium chloride (used in fertilisers and as a salt substitute), magnesium sulphate (Epsom salt, used as a bathing salt and mild laxative), calcium chloride (used to de ice roads and as a drying agent), zinc sulphate (used in dietary supplements), copper (II) sulphate (used as a fungicide in agriculture), and ammonium chloride (used in dry cell batteries and cough medicine).

questions.q: A normal salt is formed when
o: All replaceable hydrogen ions of an acid are completely replaced
No reaction between an acid and a base occurs
Only some replaceable hydrogen ions are replaced
questions.e: Normal Salts A normal salt is formed when all of the replaceable hydrogen ions of an acid are completely replaced by metal or ammonium ions, leaving no acidic hydrogen behind.

pages.title: Acid Salts
pages.body: An acid salt is formed when only some of the replaceable hydrogen ions of a polybasic acid, an acid with more than one replaceable hydrogen, are replaced, leaving at least one acidic hydrogen still present in the salt. Examples of acid salts are sodium hydrogen sulphate, sodium hydrogen carbonate, commonly known as baking soda and used in cooking, sodium hydrogen phosphate, used as a food additive, potassium hydrogen sulphate, used in some cleaning products, potassium hydrogen tartrate, also called cream of tartar and used in baking, calcium hydrogen carbonate, found dissolved in hard water, sodium hydrogen sulphite, used as a food preservative, potassium hydrogen phosphate, used as a fertiliser and food additive, ammonium hydrogen sulphate, used in some industrial processes, and monosodium phosphate, used as a food additive and buffering agent.

pages.title: Basic Salts
pages.body: A basic salt is formed when a base is only partly neutralised by an acid, so that the resulting salt still contains hydroxide ions in addition to the metal and acidic ions. Examples of basic salts are basic lead carbonate, once used as a white paint pigment, basic copper carbonate, found naturally as the green mineral malachite, basic zinc carbonate, used in some skin care products, basic magnesium carbonate, used as an antacid and food additive, basic aluminium chloride, used in some antiperspirants, basic bismuth nitrate, used in some stomach medicines, basic copper sulphate, used as a fungicide in agriculture, basic ferric sulphate, used in water treatment, basic lead acetate, historically used in some dyeing processes, and basic magnesium chloride, used in some cements.

questions.q: An acid salt is formed when
o: All hydrogen ions of an acid are replaced
Only some of the replaceable hydrogen ions of a polybasic acid are replaced
Two salts crystallise together in fixed proportion
questions.e: Acid Salts An acid salt is formed when only some of the replaceable hydrogen ions of a polybasic acid, an acid with more than one replaceable hydrogen, are replaced, leaving at least one acidic hydrogen still present in the salt.

pages.title: Double Salts
pages.body: A double salt is formed when two simple salts crystallise together in a fixed, definite proportion, producing a single crystalline compound that contains more than one type of positive or negative ion. Examples of double salts are potash alum, used in water purification and as a mordant in dyeing, ferrous ammonium sulphate, used in laboratories to prepare standard solutions, dolomite, a natural double salt of calcium and magnesium carbonate used in agriculture and construction, potassium sodium tartrate, used in baking and as a laxative, ammonium ferric sulphate, used in water treatment, chrome alum, used in tanning leather, potassium magnesium sulphate, used as a fertiliser, ammonium magnesium phosphate, found in some kidney stones, sodium potassium carbonate, used industrially, and calcium magnesium sulphate, used as a soil conditioner. Unlike acid salts and basic salts, double salts break apart into their two separate simple salts when dissolved in water.

pages.title: Physical and Chemical Properties of Salts
pages.body: Physically, most salts are crystalline solids at room temperature, ranging from colourless or white, like table salt, to strongly coloured, like blue copper (II) sulphate or green iron (II) sulphate. Many salts are soluble in water, though solubility varies considerably between different salts, and dissolved salts generally conduct electricity due to the free ions present. Chemically, salts can react with acids, bases or other salts to form new salts, and many salts, such as copper (II) sulphate crystals, contain water of crystallisation, which can be driven off by heating to leave an anhydrous (water free) powder.

questions.q: A double salt is formed when
o: A base fails to neutralise any acid
An acid completely loses all its hydrogen
Two simple salts crystallise together in a fixed proportion
questions.e: Double Salts A double salt is formed when two simple salts crystallise together in a fixed, definite proportion, producing a single crystalline compound that contains more than one type of positive or negative ion.

pages.title: Uses of Salts
pages.body:
Salts have several specific, common uses in daily life, agriculture and industry. Sodium chloride is used to season and preserve food. Sodium hydrogen carbonate, as baking soda, is used in baking to help dough rise. Potassium nitrate is used in fertilisers to supply nitrogen and potassium to crops. Calcium sulphate, as plaster of Paris, is used to set broken bones and in building plaster. Magnesium sulphate, as Epsom salt, is used for relaxing baths and as a mild laxative. Copper (II) sulphate is used as a fungicide to protect crops from fungal disease. Ammonium chloride is used in dry cell batteries. Sodium carbonate is used to soften hard water and manufacture glass. Potassium chloride is used as a salt substitute for people managing their sodium intake. Calcium chloride is used to keep roads free of ice in cold weather.

3.7  Using Indicators to Identify Acids and Bases

An indicator is a substance that changes colour depending on whether it is in contact with an acid, a base, or a neutral solution, allowing an unknown substance to be classified quickly and safely without tasting or touching it. Litmus, methyl orange, phenolphthalein and universal indicator are four indicators commonly used in the laboratory, and a table is especially useful here, since it allows the colour changes of each indicator to be compared side by side.

| **INDICATOR** | **COLOUR IN ACID** | **COLOUR IN NEUTRAL SOLUTION** | **COLOUR IN BASE (ALKALI)** |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Litmus (blue litmus paper)** | Turns red | Stays blue | Stays blue |
| **Litmus (red litmus paper)** | Stays red | Stays red | Turns blue |
| **Methyl orange** | Red | Orange | Yellow |
| **Phenolphthalein** | Colourless | Colourless | Pink or magenta |
| **Universal indicator** | Red to orange (strong to weak acid) | Green | Blue to purple (weak to strong base) |

Universal indicator is particularly valuable because, unlike the other indicators, it produces a whole range of colours corresponding to specific pH values, allowing it to estimate not only whether a substance is acidic or basic, but roughly how strong that acid or base is.

pages.title: Common Acids, Bases and Salts and Where They are Found
pages.body:
| **CLASS** | **EXAMPLES** | **WHERE FOUND OR USED** |
|---|---|---|
| **Acids** | Hydrochloric acid, sulphuric acid, nitric acid, ethanoic acid, citric acid, lactic acid | Hydrochloric acid is in the stomach. Sulphuric acid is in car batteries. Ethanoic acid is in vinegar. Citric acid is in lime and orange. Lactic acid is in sour milk |
| **Bases** | Sodium hydroxide, potassium hydroxide, calcium hydroxide, magnesium hydroxide, ammonia solution | Sodium hydroxide and potassium hydroxide are used to make soap. Calcium hydroxide is used in whitewash and to treat acid soils. Magnesium hydroxide is in medicines that relieve stomach acid |
| **Salts** | Sodium chloride, calcium carbonate, copper (II) sulphate, potassium nitrate, ammonium sulphate | Sodium chloride is table salt. Calcium carbonate is in chalk, limestone and eggshells. Potassium nitrate and ammonium sulphate are fertilisers |

A base that dissolves in water is called an alkali. A strong acid or alkali is fully broken into ions in water, while a weak one is only partly broken into ions. Hydrochloric acid and sulphuric acid are strong acids, and ethanoic acid and citric acid are weak acids. Sodium hydroxide is a strong alkali and ammonia solution is a weak alkali.

questions.q: Which indicator turns pink or magenta in a basic solution but stays colourless in an acid?
questions.e: Phenolphthalein   Colourless   Colourless   Pink or magenta

pages.title: The pH Scale and Indicators
pages.body:
| **PH** | **NATURE OF THE SOLUTION** | **COLOUR OF UNIVERSAL INDICATOR** | **EXAMPLES** |
|---|---|---|---|
| **0 to 3** | Strongly acidic | Red | Battery acid, stomach acid, lime juice |
| **4 to 6** | Weakly acidic | Orange to yellow | Vinegar, tomato juice, rain water, milk |
| **7** | Neutral | Green | Pure water, salt solution |
| **8 to 10** | Weakly alkaline | Blue | Baking soda solution, soap solution, sea water |
| **11 to 14** | Strongly alkaline | Purple | Limewater, sodium hydroxide solution |

| **INDICATOR** | **COLOUR IN ACID** | **COLOUR IN NEUTRAL SOLUTION** | **COLOUR IN ALKALI** |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Litmus** | Red | Purple | Blue |
| **Methyl orange** | Red | Orange | Yellow |
| **Phenolphthalein** | Colourless | Colourless | Pink |
| **Universal indicator** | Red to yellow | Green | Blue to purple |

To make a model of the pH scale, draw a strip with fifteen boxes numbered 0 to 14 and colour them from red through green to purple. Test household liquids with universal indicator paper and write the name of each liquid under the box that matches its colour.

pages.title: Going further
pages.body:
> 💡 **Going further**

Acids and bases react together in a process called neutralisation, in which the acidic and basic properties cancel each other out, producing a salt and water as products. This reaction is the basis for producing many of the salts described in this lesson, and also explains everyday remedies, such as taking an antacid, a mild base, to help neutralise excess stomach acid.

lessons.subject: sci
lessons.title: Chemical Bonding, Ionic, Covalent and Metallic

pages.title: What you will learn
pages.body:
🎯 **By the end of this lesson you will be able to:**
- Identify types of interatomic bonds.
- Describe the formation of interatomic bonds.
- Identify examples of substances that exhibit ionic, covalent and metallic bonding.

pages.title: What is a Chemical Bond?
pages.body:
A chemical bond is a force of attraction that holds atoms together within a compound, resulting from the behaviour of electrons in the outermost shell of each atom involved. Atoms generally form chemical bonds in order to achieve a more stable arrangement of electrons, usually by gaining, losing or sharing electrons to complete their outermost shell. Ionic bonding, covalent bonding and metallic bonding are the three main types of chemical bond studied at this level, and this lesson treats each one fully in turn, covering its formation, its properties, and example substances, before moving on to the next.

4.3  Ionic Bonding

questions.q: A chemical bond is best described as
o: A colour change in a substance
A force of attraction that holds atoms together in a compound
A physical mixture with no attraction between particles
The boiling point of a substance
questions.e: A chemical bond is a force of attraction that holds atoms together within a compound, resulting from the behaviour of electrons in the outermost shell of each atom involved.

pages.title: How Ionic Bonds Form
pages.body: An ionic bond forms when one atom, usually a metal, transfers one or more electrons completely to another atom, usually a nonmetal. The atom that loses electrons becomes a positively charged ion, called a cation, while the atom that gains electrons becomes a negatively charged ion, called an anion. Since opposite charges attract, the resulting cation and anion are held tightly together by a strong electrostatic force of attraction, and this force of attraction is the ionic bond. In sodium chloride, for example, each sodium atom transfers one electron to a chlorine atom, producing a sodium ion and a chloride ion, which then attract each other strongly.

pages.title: Properties of Ionic Compounds
pages.body: Ionic compounds share a recognisable set of properties that follow directly from their bonding. They generally form hard, crystalline solids at room temperature, since the ions are arranged in a strong, regular, repeating structure called a lattice. They have high melting and boiling points, because a great deal of energy is needed to break apart the strong attraction between the ions. Ionic compounds are often brittle, since a small shift in the layers of ions can bring similarly charged ions next to each other, causing them to repel and the crystal to shatter. Most ionic compounds dissolve in water, and when dissolved, or when melted, they conduct electricity well, since the ions are then free to move and carry charge, while a solid ionic compound does not conduct electricity, since its ions are fixed in place.

questions.q: An ionic bond forms mainly through
o: Electrons moving freely among fixed metal ions
Sharing of electron pairs between atoms
Transfer of electrons from one atom to another
questions.e: How Ionic Bonds Form An ionic bond forms when one atom, usually a metal, transfers one or more electrons completely to another atom, usually a nonmetal.

questions.q: Which property is typical of ionic compounds?
questions.e: Properties of Covalent Compounds Simple molecular covalent substances typically have low melting and boiling points, since only weak forces exist between separate molecules, even though the covalent bonds within each molecule are…

pages.title: Examples of Ionic Compounds
pages.body:
Common substances held together mainly by ionic bonding include sodium chloride, common table salt, magnesium oxide, used in heat resistant furnace linings, calcium chloride, used to melt ice on roads, potassium bromide, once used in medicine, sodium fluoride, added to toothpaste and some water supplies, calcium oxide, known as quicklime and used in cement, magnesium chloride, used in some de icing products, potassium iodide, added to table salt to prevent iodine deficiency, aluminium oxide, found naturally as the mineral corundum, and lithium fluoride, used in some specialised optical equipment.

4.4  Covalent Bonding

pages.title: How Covalent Bonds Form
pages.body: A covalent bond forms when two atoms, usually both nonmetals, share one or more pairs of electrons between them, rather than one atom transferring electrons completely to the other. Each shared pair of electrons is attracted to the nucleus of both atoms at the same time, and this shared attraction holds the atoms together. Some covalent substances, called simple molecular substances, exist as small, individual molecules, such as water or carbon (IV) oxide. Others, called giant covalent substances, form enormous, continuous networks of covalently bonded atoms, such as diamond, in which every carbon atom is bonded to four others in a continuous three dimensional structure.

questions.q: A covalent bond forms mainly through
o: Complete transfer of electrons between atoms
Free moving electrons among metal ions
Sharing of electron pairs between atoms
questions.e: 4.4  Covalent Bonding How Covalent Bonds Form A covalent bond forms when two atoms, usually both nonmetals, share one or more pairs of electrons between them, rather than one atom transferring electrons completely to the other.

pages.title: Properties of Covalent Compounds
pages.body: Simple molecular covalent substances typically have low melting and boiling points, since only weak forces exist between separate molecules, even though the covalent bonds within each molecule are themselves strong. This is why many covalent substances, such as water, oxygen and carbon (IV) oxide, exist as liquids or gases at room temperature. Simple molecular covalent substances generally do not conduct electricity, since there are no free ions or electrons available to carry charge. Giant covalent substances, by contrast, such as diamond and silicon (IV) oxide, have extremely high melting points and are extremely hard, since breaking the structure means breaking a great many strong covalent bonds throughout the entire network.

pages.title: Examples of Covalent Compounds
pages.body:
Common substances held together mainly by covalent bonding include water, essential for drinking and all life processes, carbon (IV) oxide, produced by respiration and burning, oxygen gas, needed for respiration, methane, the main component of natural gas and biogas, ammonia, used in cleaning products and fertiliser manufacture, hydrogen chloride gas, which dissolves in water to form hydrochloric acid, nitrogen gas, which makes up most of the air, diamond, a giant covalent form of pure carbon prized for its hardness, graphite, another giant covalent form of carbon used in pencils and as a lubricant, and silicon (IV) oxide, a giant covalent compound found in sand and glass.

4.5  Metallic Bonding

questions.q: Simple molecular covalent substances typically have
questions.e: Properties of Covalent Compounds Simple molecular covalent substances typically have low melting and boiling points, since only weak forces exist between separate molecules, even though the covalent bonds within each molecule are…

questions.q: Diamond and silicon (IV) oxide are examples of
questions.e: Examples of Covalent Compounds Common substances held together mainly by covalent bonding include water, essential for drinking and all life processes, carbon (IV) oxide, produced by respiration and burning, oxygen gas, needed…

pages.title: How Metallic Bonds Form
pages.body: A metallic bond forms when metal atoms release some of their outermost electrons, which then become free to move throughout the whole structure rather than staying attached to any single atom. This creates a regular arrangement of positively charged metal ions surrounded by a moving sea of delocalised (free moving) electrons. The strong attraction between the fixed positive metal ions and this surrounding sea of negative electrons is the metallic bond, and it extends throughout the entire piece of metal rather than existing between just two specific atoms.

pages.title: Properties of Metallic Substances
pages.body: Metallic substances conduct electricity and heat very well, since the delocalised electrons are free to move and carry both charge and thermal energy through the structure. Metals are generally malleable, meaning they can be hammered or pressed into different shapes, and ductile, meaning they can be drawn out into wires, since the layers of metal ions can slide over one another without breaking the overall metallic bond. Most metals have relatively high melting and boiling points, and most have a characteristic shiny (lustrous) appearance when freshly cut or polished.

questions.q: A metallic bond forms mainly through
o: Complete transfer of electrons between two atoms only
Delocalised electrons moving freely among fixed positive metal ions
No bonding at all between atoms
Sharing of electron pairs only between two atoms
questions.e: In metallic bonding, electrons are not held by any single atom at all, but move freely throughout the whole structure, surrounding a fixed arrangement of positively charged metal ions.

questions.q: Which property is typical of metallic substances?
o: Inability to be shaped at all
The ability to conduct electricity well
questions.e: Properties of Metallic Substances Metallic substances conduct electricity and heat very well, since the delocalised electrons are free to move and carry both charge and thermal energy through the structure.

pages.title: Examples of Metallic Substances
pages.body:
Common substances held together mainly by metallic bonding include iron, used in construction and tool making, copper, used in electrical wiring due to its excellent conductivity, aluminium, used in cooking pots and aeroplane bodies due to its light weight, gold, used in jewellery due to its resistance to corrosion, silver, used in jewellery and electrical contacts, zinc, used to coat (galvanise) iron to prevent rusting, sodium, a soft, reactive metal used in street lamps, magnesium, used in lightweight alloys, brass, an alloy of copper and zinc used in musical instruments and fittings, and steel, an alloy of iron and carbon used extensively in construction.

4.6  Practical Illustration

[[pic:Three side by side diagrams. The first shows an ionic bond forming between a sodium atom and a chlorine atom, with an arrow showing an electron transferring and the resulting Na+ and Cl- ions attracting. The second shows a covalent bond forming between two hydrogen atoms, with a shared pair of electrons drawn between them. The third shows a metallic structure, a grid of positive metal ion circles surrounded by small scattered dots representing a sea of delocalised electrons.]]

Notice that in ionic bonding, an electron moves completely from one atom to another, creating two oppositely charged ions that attract each other. In covalent bonding, electrons are shared between atoms rather than transferred. In metallic bonding, electrons are not held by any single atom at all, but move freely throughout the whole structure, surrounding a fixed arrangement of positively charged metal ions.

pages.title: Going further
pages.body:
> 💡 **Going further**

The type of bonding in a substance strongly influences its physical properties, which is why scientists and engineers consider bonding type when selecting materials for a specific purpose. For example, the strong metallic bonding in copper, combined with its free moving electrons, makes it an excellent material for electrical wiring, while the strong ionic bonding in compounds like magnesium oxide makes them useful as heat resistant materials in furnace linings, and the giant covalent structure of diamond makes it the hardest naturally occurring material, useful for cutting tools.

questions.e: Water is made of hydrogen and oxygen, carbon (IV) oxide is made of carbon and oxygen, iron (II) sulphide is made of iron and sulphur, and magnesium oxide is made of magnesium and oxygen.

questions.q: An element is best described as
o: A pure substance made of only one type of atom
